report.summary: Incident S06 is inconclusive: the system determination is that contradicting evidence makes up 56% of weighed evidence against a 35% maximum, so no root cause is asserted. The strongest candidate (H1) is an inventory-db replication break at about 12:59:32Z with the endpoint resolving to read-only standby db-inv-2, which is awaiting manual promotion, and inventory reservation UPDATEs failing with SQLSTATE 25006 from 13:00:29Z. H2 (inventory-service misconfigured to write to the standby) fits the same error signature and is not excluded, because no connection-string or DSN evidence was retrieved. The 15% inventory and 7% checkout error rates cannot be reconciled with the roughly 40 sampled ERROR lines, and checkout's link to inventory rests on timing only. The primary db-inv-1 was never observed directly, and the DNS, config and approval records were not obtained within the investigation budget. Mitigation should focus on restoring a writable primary and confirming write routing, pending the checks listed in open_questions.

ranked_hypotheses.mechanism: The replication stream from primary db-inv-1 broke at about 12:59:32Z (lag rose from 0.3s to 48s, connections dropped from 93 to 20 at 13:00), and the endpoint now resolves to standby db-inv-2, which is read-only and awaiting manual promotion. Inventory UPDATE stock_reservations statements fail with SQLSTATE 25006 from 13:00:29Z while reads and the liveness check still succeed.

brief.title: stock reservation failures
brief.alert: ALERT [P2] inventory-service error rate 15% since ~13:00 UTC; stock reservations failing at checkout. inventory-service health checks are green.

plan.incident_understanding: inventory-service error rate rose to about 15% since roughly 13:00 UTC, causing stock reservation failures at checkout-service. Health checks are green, so the fault is likely partial (specific operations, data paths, or downstream dependency) rather than the process being down. Telemetry covers 12:00-13:30 UTC; change history covers a longer window.
candidate_explanations: A deployment or config change to inventory-service around 13:00 UTC introduced a regression in the reservation path
A downstream dependency of inventory-service (database, cache, or another service) degraded, causing reservation calls to fail intermittently
A feature flag or configuration change altered reservation logic or timeouts, affecting only a subset of requests
Traffic or data-contention spike (e.g. hot SKUs, lock contention) causing reservation conflicts that surface as errors, possibly amplified by checkout retries

findings.summary: inventory-service error rate jumped from ~0.2% to ~15% at 13:00:00Z, and checkout-service error rate jumped from ~0.3% to ~7% at the same bucket. The inventory ERROR lines are almost all 'UPDATE stock_reservations failed: cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction (SQLSTATE 25006)', which points to a database write-path problem (read-only database or replica), not to inventory-service's own resources. Latency and CPU stayed flat through the onset. Checkout has no error log lines matching the reservation failure, so its error increase is only visible in metrics. Caveat: the log query returned only the 50 most severe lines, so the ERROR count is truncated at 40.

observations.statement: inventory-service error_rate was flat at 0.15–0.21% from 12:00 to 12:55, then rose to 15.43% at 13:00:00Z. It peaked at 15.85% at 13:05 and was 14.93% at 13:30.
checkout-service error_rate was flat at 0.26–0.36% from 12:00 to 12:55, then rose to 6.87% at 13:00:00Z. It was 7.05% at 13:30, the last point.
inventory-service latency_p99_ms stayed in the 86–93 ms range for the whole window. There is no latency rise before the 13:00 error onset, and no sustained rise after it.
checkout-service latency_p99_ms stayed in the 307–333 ms range for the whole window, with no change at 13:00.
inventory-service cpu_pct (28.8–31.1%) and memory_pct (87.8–94.3%) show no step change at 13:00. Memory has been high since 12:00 and is not related to the onset.
inventory-service request_rate stayed at 134–146 req/s across the window, with no spike at the onset. Checkout request_rate stayed at 82–88 req/s.

The first inventory ERROR line is at 13:00:29Z, 'UPDATE stock_reservations failed: ERROR: cannot execute UPDATE in a read-only transaction (SQLSTATE 25006)'. Errors then recur roughly every 30–90 s through 13:30:00Z, the last at 13:30:00Z.

Of the 50 WARN/ERROR lines returned, 40 are ERROR lines, and all 40 are the read-only-transaction UPDATE failure on stock_reservations. The other 10 WARN lines are high-heap warnings (91% of 1Gi) and cache-miss storms for SKU prefixes (for example ea62b42c at 70 misses/s, 93cb3a81 at 80/s, 7982fce7 at 82/s). The cache-miss storms are spread across different SKU prefixes and are all before or around onset.
The error lines carry no SKU, warehouse, HTTP status, or endpoint fields, so concentration by SKU, warehouse, or request pattern cannot be determined from these logs.

Checkout-service has only 2 WARN/ERROR lines in the window: a slow inventory reservation of 1147 ms at 12:26:08Z (before onset), and a card-declined rejection at 12:48:57Z (unrelated to inventory). A reservation-keyword INFO search for 12:55–13:15 returned nothing. Checkout's ~7% error rate therefore has no matching log lines.
Before 13:00 the only inventory warnings were heap and cache-miss warnings, with no reservation or DB write errors. The first DB write error came after the 13:00:00 metric step.

interpretations.statement: The stock-reservation failures starting at 13:00 are caused by inventory-service's writes being sent to a read-only database endpoint (for example, a failover or a replica promotion issue). The error text points to the database rather than to inventory-service code or capacity.

Latency and CPU did not rise before errors, so this does not look like a saturation or slowness failure that led to errors. Heap pressure and cache-miss storms predate the onset but are not correlated with the error jump and do not explain the write failures.

Checkout's error increase (~7%) is a downstream effect of inventory reservation failures (checkout error onset coincides with the inventory onset at 13:00). Checkout logs do not contain the failure text, so this link is inferred from timing only.

Errors are around 15% for inventory and 7% for checkout, which is consistent with only a subset of reservation requests (e.g. ones that write) failing, not all of them. Concentration by SKU, warehouse, or pattern is unproven.

tasks.objective: Search past incident postmortems for inventory-service reservation failures or similar partial-error patterns with green health checks, and summarise their root causes and mitigations so they can be compared with the current signature.

findings.summary: Past-incident search found one inventory-service postmortem that matches the reservation-failure pattern (P03, cache eviction storm). It is a partial match: the symptoms overlap (inventory errors, high database load), but the postmortem does not mention green health checks, and it concerns a cache memory limit rather than a stale or failing health check. A second match (P05) is about checkout TLS errors on payment-service and does not match this signature. No past incident in the index describes inventory-service reservation failures with green health checks, so there is no direct precedent to compare against. Treat P03 only as a hypothesis to test against current telemetry.

observations.statement: P03 (2026-04-03, inventory-service and inventory-cache) describes inventory errors, cache misses and high database load. Root cause: cache memory limit too low after catalogue growth. Resolution: increased cache memory and added an eviction alert.

P05 (2026-06-11, payment-service and checkout-service) describes TLS handshake failures and checkout 5xx errors. Root cause: an expired certificate from a cert-manager misconfiguration. Resolution: certificate renewed and expiry alerting added.

Three searches (inventory-service scoped, cross-service checkout scoped, and a connection-pool/deadlock query scoped to inventory-service) returned only P03 and P05. No other inventory-service postmortem was returned.

interpretations.statement: P03 is a plausible hypothesis for S06 if inventory-cache evictions or database load are rising now. Its signature (errors with high DB load) would fit a 15% error rate, but the green health checks in S06 are not explained by it, and the postmortem does not state whether its health checks were green.

P05 is unlikely to explain S06 on its own. Its failure was TLS-specific on payment-service, while S06 is an inventory-service error rate with checkout as a downstream symptom. A TLS cause would also not usually leave inventory health checks green.

Shallow health checks are a plausible reason S06 shows green checks while reservations fail. The health check may not exercise the reservation write path, as in the P03 pattern, but nothing in the past-incident data confirms this.

data_gaps: Past-incident search only returns postmortems that keyword-match. No postmortem of an inventory-service partial-error incident with green health checks was found, so the comparison rests on one partial match.

interpretations.statement: The primary endpoint pointing at a read-only standby is consistent with the reported stock reservation write failures, since reservations need writes. This is a plausible mechanism, not a confirmed one.

H1 (endpoint or failover change) is the more supported hypothesis, because the degraded state is about endpoint resolution. However, no failover or DNS change was logged in the window, so the change may have happened outside the change-tracking system or before 12:00 UTC.

H2 (config change in inventory-service database configuration) is not supported by the change records. No config_change was logged for inventory-service or inventory-db in the window, though the configuration content itself was not inspected.

inventory-service's green health check is expected to be a false negative, because it does not exercise database writes. The loud errors on inventory-service and checkout-service are consistent with inventory-service being a caller of a failing inventory-db, not the origin.

issues.detail: The replication-break errors at 12:59:32Z and 13:00:16Z are cited as contradicting H2. They do not. A misrouted writer would fail with the same read-only error regardless of why the replica lost its primary connection. The timing argument (replication break precedes first inventory error by about 30s) also does not exclude H2, because H2 only needs the endpoint to be wrong from the time of a config change. H2 is therefore not ruled out by these records.

inventory-service's actual database connection target was never inspected. Config content and DNS history were not retrieved, so the claim that no config change occurred rests only on change-history records, which the analysis itself flags as possibly incomplete for infra events. Without the connection target, H1 (endpoint switched to a read-only standby) and H2 (service pointed at the standby by config) cannot be separated.

The claim that db-inv-1 is unavailable is not verified. The replication errors are logged by inventory-db, the standby, and describe the primary as unreachable. The primary's own health and logs were never queried, so the failure could be on the primary, the network path, or the standby's replication client.

Confidence 0.60 is high given that the endpoint switch time is unknown (the 13:28 snapshot is not onset-time evidence), DNS history is missing, the primary is unexamined, and the standby promotion record is absent. The 0.60 figure should be lowered until these are checked.

The claim that checkout errors are downstream of inventory reservation failures rests on timing alone. Checkout has no ERROR lines and no inventory-related lines in the window, so its 7% error rate has no observed mechanism. A separate checkout-side cause is not excluded.

The 15% inventory error rate is not reconciled with the log volume. Roughly 8 to 40 sampled ERROR lines over 30 minutes is far below 15% of about 140 req/s, but the log query was capped at 50 lines, so the unsampled count is unknown. The mismatch is unresolved rather than proof that the metric is wrong, so the reservation-failure rate is uncertain.

Promotion of db-inv-2 was still pending at 13:03:34Z and the 13:28 snapshot shows the primary endpoint resolving to a read-only standby, which together favour H1. The critique correctly noted that replication-break logs do not discriminate against H2, since a misrouted writer would also fail with the same error, so H2 is only weakly disfavoured and its confidence is lowered. Database CPU, latency and disk stayed flat and inventory CPU and latency are unchanged, so saturation is not the origin, and the cache hypothesis lacks support for a read-only error. Checkout's 7% error rate has no matching logs and is treated as a timing-linked downstream effect only. The 15% error rate cannot be reconciled with the sampled log volume, and the primary db-inv-1 was never examined, so overall confidence is moderate at best.

DNS or endpoint resolution history for the inventory-db primary name showing when it changed to db-inv-2 and who triggered it
inventory-service connection-string and pool configuration history, plus a DSN or connection-open log showing the host used for writes

analysis.response_to_critique: [misread_evidence H2] Accepted: the replication-break lines do not contradict H2, so they were removed from H2's contradicting list and H2 is no longer dismissed on that basis. [alternative_not_ruled_out H2] Accepted: H2 cannot be separated from H1 without the connection target, and H2 remains open at 0.25. [unsupported_claim H1] Accepted: db-inv-1 unavailability is unverified, and it is now an explicit assumption. [overconfidence H1] Accepted: H1 confidence lowered from 0.60 to 0.50 given the unknown endpoint switch time, missing DNS history and unexamined primary. [unsupported_claim H1 checkout] Accepted: checkout linkage is timing-only and flagged as an assumption. [misread_evidence H1 15% reconciliation] Accepted: the log-volume mismatch is noted as unresolved and contributes to lower confidence.

critique.summary: H1 (inventory-db replication break and endpoint on read-only standby db-inv-2) is the best-supported hypothesis: inventory errors start 13:00:29Z after a 12:59:32Z replication loss, all share SQLSTATE 25006, and db-inv-2 is pending promotion. However, the analysis overstates confidence in the causal link and some claims are not backed by the ledger. The H1 mechanism that writes reached db-inv-2 is not shown in any log, and the ledger has no record of which host inventory-service writes to. The 15% and 7% error rates are not reconciled with the sampled log volume, and the checkout link rests on timing only. The primary db-inv-1 was never observed, so the claim it is down is unverified. No further investigation is possible, so the conclusion should be revised to reflect the uncertainty.

issues.detail: The analysis asserts that inventory writes are routed to read-only standby db-inv-2 and that db-inv-1 is unavailable. No ledger record shows the write connection target. The inventory connection-open and DSN lines were never retrieved (T8 budget exhausted), and db-inv-1 telemetry was never obtained (T7). The mechanism linking the replication break to the endpoint switch is inferred, not observed.

H2 (inventory-service connection target misconfigured to the standby) fits the same 25006 error signature and is not excluded. The replication break at 12:59:32Z does not discriminate between them, since a misrouted writer fails regardless of replication state. The change records are empty for the window, but the config content was never inspected, so the H2 path is open and H1 cannot be preferred on the current evidence.

The 13:28 health snapshot shows the primary endpoint currently resolves to db-inv-2. It is a single later snapshot and does not show the endpoint state at 12:59-13:00. The analysis treats it as onset-time state.

Confidence of 0.50 for H1 is stated alongside a claimed failover that no log records. The log shows only a pending promotion. The reported 15% error rate is about 10x the 8 to 40 sampled ERROR lines, which suggests either the sample is incomplete or the failure signature is broader than the 25006 write failures. The gap is not resolved.

The analysis cites M12 as contradicting, but the checkout error_rate contradiction is not weighed. Checkout reports ~7% errors with no matching ERROR or WARN lines, and the timing link is weak. The checkout dependency on inventory is not established.

Decisive evidence for the write routing (connection-open or DSN lines, DNS history, db-inv-1 health) was requested but not obtained because the budget was exhausted. These gaps cannot be closed with available tools, so the report should state that the conclusion is provisional.

reasons: contradicting evidence is 56% of the weighed evidence (max 35%)
